analysis.one_liner: Bars lawsuits against gun makers and sellers for harm caused when their products are criminally misused by others.
analysis.headline: The Senate voted 75–22 to take up the gun industry immunity bill, but debate collapsed when Democrats demanded votes on gun-control amendments, and a vote to cut off debate failed 8–90 on March 2, 2004, killing the bill.
analysis.plain_summary: Sponsored by Sen. Larry Craig, this bill would have made it illegal to sue firearm and ammunition manufacturers, dealers, and importers in any state or federal court for harms caused when someone criminally misuses a gun, and it would have immediately thrown out lawsuits already in progress. It kept narrow exceptions for cases like a dealer knowingly selling to someone likely to misuse it. Gun industry lawsuits, including ones filed by cities, would have been wiped out. The bill died on the Senate floor after a fight over amendments.
analysis.who_benefits: Firearm and ammunition manufacturers, distributors, dealers, importers, and their trade associations would gain near-total protection from civil lawsuits over criminal misuse of their products, including immunity from suits already filed. Gun buyers would keep access to a supply of firearms without the industry facing litigation costs that supporters said could squeeze the market.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gun makers, dealers, and trade associations

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any 'qualified civil liability action' — a suit against a gun or ammunition manufacturer or seller, or their trade association, for damages from criminal or unlawful misuse of the product — from being brought in any state or federal court [S2][S3].
Requires courts to immediately dismiss any such lawsuit already pending when the law takes effect [S2][S3].

Preserves exceptions, so suits remain possible against sellers who negligently hand a gun to someone likely to misuse it, sellers who knowingly broke sale or marketing laws, cases of product defect, and transfers to people the seller knew were prohibited buyers [S2][S3].
The bill's stated purposes include protecting the gun supply for lawful uses and shielding the industry from liability for harm 'solely caused by others' when products function as designed [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, victims of gun violence and the cities and counties suing gun sellers would have lost their main civil tool against the industry — pending cases would have been dismissed by law. Future victims injured through criminal misuse of a functioning gun would have had no negligence claim against the maker or seller, even where the exceptions were hard to invoke.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun violence victims and suing cities

drawbacks.text: The bill would have dismissed pending lawsuits and barred future ones by gun violence victims and municipalities, ending their ability to use courts to change how guns are sold and marketed [S2][S3].

Critics of the bill noted during the Senate debate that Democrats demanded votes on amendments to reauthorize the assault weapons ban and close the gun show background-check loophole, and would not let the bill advance without them [S5]; these amendments were not part of the bill [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge the exceptions were narrow: a victim would still have to prove the seller knowingly broke a specific law or negligently entrusted the gun, and the bill itself states criminal misuse of a gun is not 'reasonably foreseeable' for product-defect purposes, making recovery difficult [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the gun industry, the benefit was enormous and one-sided: a federal shield from nearly all misuse lawsuits, retroactively ending cases already filed. For ordinary people the cost was real — victims and cities would lose a legal avenue, and the civil courts would no longer serve as any check on how guns are marketed and sold. The bill did keep some liability for dealer misconduct and defective products, but the core of the bill was litigation immunity for an entire industry.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate broadly agreed to debate the bill, but Democrats refused to end debate until they got votes on gun-control amendments, and when a vote to cut off debate failed 8–90, the bill was dropped and never came to an up-or-down vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Larry Craig introduced the bill on October 31, 2003, with one Democratic cosponsor, and it was placed on the Senate calendar in early November [S1][S4][S5].

On February 25, 2004, the Senate voted 75–22 — including 24 of 48 Democrats and 50 of 51 Republicans — to invoke cloture on the motion to proceed, meaning to allow debate on the bill to begin [S6][S5].
After several days of floor debate, a cloture motion to cut off debate on the bill itself failed 8–90 on March 2, 2004, with 41 of 48 Democrats and 48 of 51 Republicans voting no [S7][S5].
The bill never received a final up-or-down vote and died when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun violence victims and the cities suing the industry kept their lawsuits alive, and the firearm industry went the rest of the Congress without its immunity shield. (A nearly identical law did pass and was signed the following year in the 109th Congress.)

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun violence victims and suing cities

for.name: Sen. Larry Craig
for.what_they_did: Introduced S. 1805 to bar civil liability actions against the firearms industry and promoted it on the floor.

for.name: 50 of 51 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted to invoke cloture on the motion to proceed, clearing the way for debate on the bill.

for.name: 24 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted with Republicans to allow debate on the bill to begin.

for.name: National Rifle Association
for.what_they_did: Backed the industry liability shield and pressed for its passage.

against.name: 41 of 48 Senate Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted against the cloture motion on the bill itself (8–90 final tally), refusing to end debate until they got votes on amendments to reauthorize the assault weapons ban and require background checks at gun shows.

against.name: Sen. Bill Frist
against.what_they_did: Dropped the bill from the floor after the failed vote to cut off debate, rather than bring it back up.

against.name: 48 of 51 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on the final cloture motion — a procedural move on the losing side to preserve the ability to reconsider the bill later.

sides.party_line_note: The vote to begin debate was bipartisan (75–22, with 24 Democrats and 50 Republicans in favor), but the bill was killed in a procedural vote where Democrats voted no to force amendment votes and most Republicans voted no as a maneuver to keep the bill alive.

industries.industry: Firearm and ammunition manufacturers, dealers, and importers
industries.note: The bill would have granted the industry a federal shield from lawsuits over criminal misuse of its products, retroactively dismissing suits already filed, including cases brought by cities. Victims would lose their day in court as the industry's litigation risk disappeared.
Trade associations were named as protected parties under the bill and could not be sued over misuse claims either, while the NRA actively supported passage.
The bill would have ended their pending suits and barred future ones, so their loss tracked directly with the loss of recourse for gun violence victims.
